bib.title: Coordination as an Architectural Layer for LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Coordination as an Architectural Layer for LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems: An Information-Controlled Empirical Study on Prediction Markets", Maksym Nechepurenko, Pavel Shuvalov (Devnull FZCO, Dubai). arXiv:2605.03310v1 [cs.MA], 5 May 2026. Preprint, no venue. The authors call it "a position paper paired with a methodology-validating empirical study".

COVERAGE: 92,500 of 99,608 chars read, all body text, tables and discussion. The last ~7,000 chars are references, which I skimmed and did not read in full. There are no appendices with results. Figures 4-7 are not readable in the extraction, so I used their captions and the surrounding text. Table 2 and Table 3 extracted cleanly.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. With information fixed, topology gives only small Brier differences, and none survives multiple-comparison correction. The best-to-worst spread is 0.028 Brier. The sequential pipeline ties the market baseline and every other configuration is worse.
 number: Brier 0.153 (sequential pipeline), 0.159 (independent ensemble), 0.162 (orchestrator-specialist), 0.170 (peer-critique debate), 0.181 (consensus alignment); market 0.152
 setup: claude-opus-4-6, temperature 0.3, 100 post-cutoff Polymarket binary markets, web search disabled, same tools, same prompt scaffold, 1,500-token per-call output cap. N=3 peers, debate R=2, consensus R=3 with tolerance 0.05.
 quote: "The aggregate ranking is sequential_pipeline<independent_ensemble≈orchestra-tor_specialist<peer_critique_debate<consensus_alignment, with the spread between best and worst at 0.028 Brier units."
 where: Sec 6.1, Table 2, p16-17
2. No pair of configurations is significant after correction. The smallest uncorrected p-values are 0.075 to 0.082, all for consensus alignment against another configuration. The Bonferroni threshold is p<0.005.
 number: p=0.075, 0.080, 0.082; 10 pairs
 setup: paired t-tests on per-market squared error, n=94 markets common to all configurations
 quote: "No pair reaches p <0.05 uncorrected, and the Bonferroni-corrected threshold across 10 pairs is p <0.005."
 where: Sec 6.3, p18
3. Consensus alignment is the one configuration that separates from the rest. Its 95% bootstrap intervals exclude zero against three configurations, but the 99% intervals all straddle zero. The authors call this exploratory.
 number: bootstrap p of 0.023, 0.024, 0.020; 10,000 resamples; n=94
 quote: "three pairs (consensus_alignmentvssequential_pipeline, vsindependent_ensemble, vs orchestrator_specialist) have 95% bootstrap CIs that exclude zero"
 where: Sec 6.6, p20
4. The cost differences are far larger than the quality differences, and two configurations form the Pareto frontier. Independent ensemble ($0.10 per market, Brier 0.159) and sequential pipeline ($0.36, Brier 0.153) are non-dominated. Orchestrator-specialist ($0.31, 0.162) and debate ($0.23, 0.170) cost more than the ensemble and score worse. Consensus alignment ($0.10, 0.181) is dominated at the same cost.
 number: tokens per market 55,253 / 15,362 / 49,215 / 36,015 / 15,113; the pipeline uses about 3.6x and the orchestrator about 3.2x the ensemble's tokens
 setup: same as claim 1. Compute is endogenous, not held constant. Total cost was $109.65 and wall time 3h09m. The authors say cost is partly architecture and partly implementation, for example prompt caching.
 quote: "orchestrator-specialist and peer-critique-debate are dominated by independent ensemble on the observed cost–quality frontier."
 where: Sec 6.4, p19; Table 2
5. The authors state that a single Brier number hides the architectural signal. Configurations whose Brier scores differ by less than one SEM sit in distinct regions of reliability (REL) and resolution (RES) space under the Murphy decomposition (Brier = UNC + REL − RES).
 number: REL/RES: pipeline 0.013/0.109, ensemble 0.020/0.110, orchestrator 0.025/0.112, debate 0.020/0.100, consensus 0.026/0.094. UNC=0.249.
 setup: K=10 decile bins, about 10 markets per bin. The authors say the REL and RES points are noisy and shown without confidence regions.
 quote: "Table 2 alone shows configurations whose Brier scores differ by less than the per-configuration SEM, but Figure 4 shows them occupying distinct regions of REL–RES space."
 where: Sec 7.1, p24. This is a weak claim, because the SEM of alpha is 0.011-0.015.
6. Of five pre-specified failure-signature predictions, three are upheld and two are not. The ensemble (moderate REL, high RES) and consensus alignment (lowest RES, 0.094) are upheld. Debate is partially upheld. The orchestrator is contradicted, with the highest REL (0.025) where low was predicted. The pipeline matches only its best-case branch.
 quote: "Three predictions out of five are upheld in spirit; one (orchestrator-specialist) is contradicted in direction; one (sequential pipeline) corresponds to the prediction's best-case branch"
 where: Sec 6.2, p17-18. The predictions were timestamped in Git (tag paper-v05, commit 3047e1d, 2026-04-27) but were not formally pre-registered.
7. No configuration beat the market, so all alphas are negative. The authors say this is not a verdict on coordination. It reflects the information regime: with web search off, the agent has nothing beyond the price history the market already encodes.
 number: alpha −0.001 (pipeline) to −0.028 (consensus); market Brier 0.152
 quote: "No configuration produces positive Alpha on this fixture"
 where: Sec 6.1, 7.3, p16, 25
8. Topology effects depend on the task category (exploratory, about 17 markets per category). Sports Brier spread is 0.012. Economics spread is 0.121, from 0.120 (pipeline) to 0.241 (debate).
 quote: "Sports markets show essentially no separation between configurations (0.012 spread); economics markets show a ∼6× larger spread (0.121)."
 where: Sec 6.5, Table 3, p20. The authors say it is too underpowered to claim formally.
9. Case studies of failure modes (not selected for) match the predictions. Debate and consensus alignment collapsed to p=0.12 and 0.15 where three other configurations said 0.55-0.85 (market 66). Consensus alignment converged at 0.35 where four configurations were at 0.83-0.87 (market 92). The pipeline output 0.25 where four configurations said 0.50 (market 32).
 where: Sec 6.8, p23-24
10. The sample needed to resolve the pairs is large. Detecting an alpha difference of 0.02 takes about 350 paired observations. The four consensus-alignment pairs need n of 387-483. The other pairs need 1,120-2,514. Ensemble against orchestrator is indistinguishable, with an observed difference of +0.0002.
 quote: "A follow-up at n≈500 would resolve all four at the Bonferroni-corrected threshold α = 0.005 with power 0.80."
 where: Sec 6.6, p22
11. The authors cite Ao et al. (2026) for a non-identifiability result. Differences in tools, context or transcript length between architectures cannot be attributed to coordination. They say no published multi-agent study satisfies the information-fixing requirement.
 quote: "any observed gain may reflect added information rather than improved delegation."
 where: Sec 2.3, p4-5. This is a citation of Ao et al., not a result of this paper.
12. Context claims the authors cite from other work, not tested here. Multi-agent systems fail in production at "between 41% and 87%" (Cemri et al., 2025). MAST: 14 failure modes across 1600+ traces, 79% from specification and coordination issues. Xu et al. (2026) report that single-agent baselines with the same tools and context often match multi-agent designs at lower cost.
 where: Sec 1-2.1, p2-4

Framework (conceptual): three layers (information, coordination, agent). The coordination layer is defined by seven elements: endpoints, topology graph, authority distribution, synchronization, aggregation, termination, failure handling. Principle 1 fixes the model, tools, prompt template, per-call cap and question set. Principle 2 says total compute is an endogenous output, not held constant.

LIMITS
- One model (claude-opus-4-6), one task family (binary forecasting), one tool stack, web search disabled, n=100 with 494/500 successful predictions.
- The task is effectively "calibrate against the market price", because the agent sees the baseline price and price history. The authors concede the agents "have nothing additional to bring".
- Nothing is significant after Bonferroni correction. The bootstrap finding is exploratory.
- Role prompts were written once with no ablation. Cost partly reflects implementation, such as caching.
- Predictions were not formally pre-registered.
- Cross-model replication, web-search-enabled replication (the Foresight Arena live channel) and a larger n are all deferred, with no results reported.
- The authors say they "anticipate" the negative-alpha result "will not generalise" to tool-augmented settings.
- The text calls the orchestrator the single-point-error candidate, but only the debate and consensus case studies are shown. The pipeline case study is on a market with no information.
- Two authors from one company, no peer review. The authors disclose that Claude Opus 4.7 was used for editing, literature synthesis and figure rendering, and Claude Code for the harness.

BUILDS ON (as printed)
- Ao, Gao and Simchi-Levi (2026), on information versus architecture non-identifiability. Their method is the design basis.
- Cemri et al. (2025), MAST failure taxonomy.
- Acharya (2026), semantic intent divergence.
- Wynn et al. (2025), debate suppresses minority views.
- Xu et al. (2026) and Xia et al. (2024), single-agent baselines.
- Agashe et al. (2025), LLM-Coordination, in Findings of ACL NAACL.
- Daunis et al. (2025), Cao et al. (2026), Hu et al. (2025, AWS Strands) and Microsoft (2026), declarative orchestration.
- Classical coordination: Gelernter (1985), Hoare (1985), Milner (1999), Hewitt et al. (1973), Gamma et al. (1994).
- Scoring: Brier (1950), Murphy (1973), Gneiting and Raftery (2007), DeGroot and Fienberg (1983).
- Forecasting with LLMs: Schoenegger and Park (2023), Halawi et al. (2024), Schoenegger et al. (2024), Zou et al. (2024).
- Nechepurenko and Shuvalov (2026), the Foresight Arena companion paper, supplies the Alpha Score and the power analysis.
- Gelman and Carlin (2014), Type-S and Type-M errors.

CODE: none worth keeping. The harness is in TypeScript at github.com/ForesightFlow/coordination-experiment (tag paper-v05). The traces are at ForesightFlow/datasets, coordination-traces-100 (about 17.1M tokens, CC-BY 4.0).

FIGURES (one candidate)
- Figure 5, p19: "Cost–quality Pareto frontier on Phase 0.5 (n = 100 per configuration). The dashed line connects non-dominated configurations. Independent ensemble dominates orchestrator-specialist and peer-critique-debate on cost-adjusted accuracy; sequential pipeline achieves the lowest Brier at the highest cost." It shows at a glance that topology moves cost more than quality. A simple table of Table 2's Brier and cost columns could replace it.
- Other candidate: Figure 2, p9, the five topologies diagram.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions found.
- Extraction mangled spacing in some words (for example "mostexistingmulti-agentcomparisonsconfound...") and the bullet runs "≈", "<" and the table cells run together. I corrected none of the quotes, but check the spacing if pasting them.
- The vector figures (4-7) have no extractable data.
- Table 3 "overall" for the pipeline (0.151) differs from Table 2 (0.153), which the paper explains by the fallback predictions.
- The "p-value" and bootstrap "p" figures are not the same quantity. The 0.020-0.024 values are bootstrap probabilities, not t-test p-values.
